title: Uways al-Qarani
hook: a man from Yemen who never met the Prophet ﷺ, cared for his mother, and whose prayers were sought
tomorrow: The women who asked for a day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sa'd, the chief of the Ansar. Your line was: the throne shook. In which one role did you try to be sincere? Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

Every time a fresh group of fighters arrives in Medina from Yemen, Umar ibn al-Khattab goes out to meet them with the same question. Is Uways ibn Amir among you? Again and again, no. Umar leads the whole community by now, with no shortage of other business. And still he keeps asking after one man, a man he has never seen. Then one day a voice in the crowd says yes. Umar walks up to him and asks his own favor: pray for me. Today: Uways al-Qarani.
screen: `IS UWAYS AMONG YOU?` → `AGAIN AND AGAIN, NO.` → `THEN ONE DAY, YES.`

segments.voice: The story is in Sahih Muslim, and Umar tells us why he kept asking. He had heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, describe a man who would come with the reinforcements from Yemen: Uways ibn Amir, of the tribe of Murad, then of the clan of Qaran. He had suffered a skin disease and been cured of it, except for one small patch. And he had a mother, and he was devoted to her. Then the Prophet said something remarkable: if this man swore by God, God would make his oath come true. If you meet him, ask him to seek forgiveness for you. So Umar checks every detail, one by one, and Uways confirms them all. Murad, Qaran, the healed skin, the mother. Then Umar, the companion of the Prophet, asks a man who never met the Prophet to pray for him. And Uways does. Why did he never meet him? The hadith only says he had a mother and was dutiful to her. Tradition says that is exactly what kept him in Yemen: she needed him, and he stayed. Hold that part as the tradition's telling, not the hadith's words. Then comes the end of the conversation, which is easy to miss. Umar asks where he is going. Kufa, says Uways. Umar offers to write to the governor there for him. And Uways declines. He says he would rather be among the ordinary people, the ones nobody notices. He had a recommendation from the leader of the believers in his hand, and he let it go. Look at the shape of it. The man whose prayer was sought was the man who did not seek to be seen. In the Prophet's description, the one deed named is not a battle or a speech. It is his care for his mother.
screen: `DESCRIBED BY THE PROPHET.` · `DEVOTED TO HIS MOTHER.` · `UMAR ASKS HIM TO PRAY.` · `HE CHOOSES TO STAY UNNOTICED.` · then, large: `HE STAYED WITH HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: care for a parent today. Let your breath slow down. Bring your mother or father to mind, or whoever raised you. Breathe in, and think of one ordinary thing they need right now. A call. A ride. A meal. Their medicine picked up. Ten minutes of listening without checking your phone. Breathe out, and decide on that one thing. If your parent has died, you can hold them in mind instead, and if you pray, you can ask mercy for them. If the relationship is hard, you can choose something small and safe, or simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Uways al-Qarani. A man of Qaran in Yemen, devoted to his mother, described by the Prophet, and sought out by Umar for his prayer. Today's word.
Your line: he stayed with his mother. Today, do the one thing you chose for a parent, and don't post about it. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the report in Sahih Muslim of Umar seeking out Uways and asking for his prayer, and often hold him up as an example of devotion to a parent and of a hidden, humble life.

fork.setup: you're Uways. Umar, leader of the believers, offers to write a letter to the governor of Kufa for you. what do you do?
options: take the letter and go straight to the governor.
thank him and decline: you'd rather be among ordinary people.

fork.reveal: Muslim reports he declined, preferring to be among the ordinary people. the man whose prayer was sought didn't seek to be seen.

original.note: Arabic: Uways, of the clan of Qaran.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saintly hermit from a folk tale.
what it means: a real report in Sahih Muslim: the Prophet described him, and Umar sought him out to ask for his prayer.
what a scholar hears: the honor rests on his devotion to his mother, and the report ends with him turning down a letter of recommendation.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2542 (the Prophet describes Uways; Umar seeks him from the Yemeni reinforcements; Uways declines the letter to Kufa)

notes: All details are paraphrased from Sahih Muslim 2542 (and its variant chains); hadith number cited from memory, please confirm.

The outline's hook says he never met the Prophet because he was caring for his mother. Muslim states his devotion to his mother but not the causal link explicitly; the script attributes the link to tradition. Confirm framing.
'Leader of the believers' (amir al-mu'minin) for Umar and 'fighters/reinforcements' (amdad) from Yemen: confirm wording.
The patch of skin is described in the hadith as the size of a dirham; the script says 'one small patch'.

Editor pass: cut the unsupported 'small clan', 'nobody in Medina has seen' and 'an empire's worth of letters' from the hook; cut 'Muslims have often told it that way' (unsourced 'often' claim); softened 'praised him for one thing above all' to what the report names; varied the practice opener.
Practice adds a gentle alternative for listeners with hard parental relationships; confirm appropriateness.
